Journal of Human Resources, 57(S), S167-S199. — This study provides direct empirical estimates of employer concentration across U.S. local labor markets and its effects on wages and employment. Analyzing its results for wage pass-through and employment stability under minimum wage changes can help confirm or refute whether high concentration reduces net earnings gains.

[PATH:empirical] Card, D., & Krueger, A. B. (1994). 'Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania.' American Economic Review, 84(4), 772-793. — Classic minimum wage study that can be re-examined with concentration measures. Replicating its analysis while incorporating local employer concentration data (e.g., from the Census or LEHD) can test whether employment stability effects differ in concentrated markets, affecting net earnings.

[PATH:theoretical] Manning, A. (2003). Monopsony in Motion: Imperfect Competition in Labor Markets. Princeton University Press. — This foundational theoretical work models monopsony power and its implications for wage and employment responses. Extending its framework to explicitly incorporate employment stability and dynamic earnings paths can provide testable predictions about whether high concentration dampens net gains from minimum wage increases.
